repairs.original_deletion_text_preserved: Communication outages interrupt both access to hydrological forecasts and the observations needed to update them. Crowdsourced reports offer additional information but may be correlated or controlled by one attacker. This study examines a browser deployment framework that separates local forecasting from report delivery and evaluates evidence aggregation under explicit adversarial assumptions. The revised forecasting protocol replaces a constructed disaster risk index with daily regional ERA5-Land runoff depth in Vietnam and a supplementary observed discharge benchmark from WaterBench-Iowa. Temporal attention LSTM models, including a variant trained with censored recent inputs, are compared with persistence, seasonal persistence, seasonal decomposition and a nonnegative forecast combination that accounts for error bias and covariance. Forecast accuracy, interruption sensitivity and browser execution are distinct evaluation questions. A completed synthetic verification experiment comprises 71 configurations and 1,000 matched trials per configuration, comparing six aggregation methods and three feedback regimes. In one prespecified configuration with five high-reputation honest reporters and twenty neutral-reputation attackers, pooling repeated evidence by geographic and temporal group reduces false alerts but leaves missed alerts and abstentions; feedback based on the system's own decisions can defeat this protection.
